His father had never once admitted his mother was right about anything, not the dishwasher loading, not the route to Ania's cabin. He read the message again. A man who would rather lend the government money all year than risk owing a cent in April, saying probably. He typed back: What do I do?

Do what you think. You're going to make your own mistakes either way.

That was the closest thing to a blessing his father issued. Owen pocketed the phone and stood in the bleach hallway, and it occurred to him that he had spent seventeen years assuming there was a correct answer to everything, some ledger he'd be graded against, and that the adults he trusted had mostly been guessing too. Caylee would say claim nothing, keep every dollar now. Ania would say the withholding system exists so you don't get crushed in April. Both of them would be certain, and Owen envied that, and did not share it.

Back in the office, Mr. Moose was signing something with a pen that had a feather on it, for reasons Owen decided not to ask about. "Figured out your W-4?" he said. "Half these kids make their parents fill it out and bring it back. One kid tried to have his mother fax it. We don't even have a fax machine. I had to exhume the old one from storage just so he could feel heard."

"I filled it out myself," Owen said, and it was true, he had, in the hallway, one line at a time. "I'm still not sure I chose right."

"Nobody's sure," Mr. Moose said. "You'll find out in April." He held up an apron, red, folded. "You start Saturday, eight in the morning. Bagging, carts, spills. There will be spills."

Owen took the apron. It was heavier than he expected, like it had already absorbed a decade of other people's work. Outside, in the parking lot, he texted Ania first, then thought better of the wisdom he'd been drafting, and just wrote: got the job. She sent back a cartwheel emoji and the message, does this mean employee discount on ice cream.

"Yes," he said out loud, to nobody, and put the apron on over his shirt right there in the lot, tags and all.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
Nada's kitchen smelled of cardamom and burnt toast, which was the usual state of things, and Angel had already claimed the good chair by the window before Chase got his backpack off. The assignment sat between them like a dare: one short news article in Spanish, read aloud, then summarised in your own words, recorded and submitted by Sunday night. Nada had done hers on Tuesday. Angel had done hers during homeroom. Chase had put it off until Saturday, which was why he was here, at Nada's table, with his phone propped against a sugar jar like a witness.

"Pick a short one," Nada said, scrolling through the news site on his laptop. "Two paragraphs, tops. You stumble less when it's short."

"Thanks for the confidence."

"I'm being realistic. You said yourself you froze on the last quiz."

He hadn't said it exactly that way, but he didn't argue. He leaned over her shoulder as she skimmed headlines, and then he saw one, and stopped scrolling with two fingers on the trackpad. He read it three times, and the words he knew assembled themselves slowly: plant, town, three hundred. Nada watched his face rather than the screen, which was a habit of hers that he both appreciated and resented.

"That one," he said. "That's the one I'm doing."

"You don't know half those words."

"Then I'll learn them." He pulled the laptop toward himself and began copying the article into his notes, sounding out syllables under his breath while Angel looked up from her drawing and gave him a noncommittal shrug, as if to say it was his funeral.

The trouble came quickly, and it came in a single word. Según. It appeared in the second sentence, right before a claim that the plant would close by spring, and then again further down, before a number. Chase had a vague feeling about it, something from a Tuesday in September, but the feeling wouldn't resolve into meaning. He typed it into a translator, which offered him "according to," and then, unhelpfully, a dozen example sentences that all raised more questions than they answered. The article said según el alcalde. It said según la empresa. But what the article itself said, what the reporter was willing to stand behind, he could not tell from the translator, and the difference seemed suddenly enormous.

"You're staring," Angel said.

"I'm working."

"You're stewing. There's a difference." She came around the table and read over his shoulder, lips moving. "My cousin talks like this. Según mi mamá, según el doctor. It's like, this is what they say."

"So it's not a fact."

"I didn't say that. I said it's what they say." She went back to her drawing, having deposited exactly enough information to make everything more complicated.

Chase read the sentence again. The plant would close, según el alcalde. He thought about how the English version would run in their own local paper: "The plant will close by spring, according to the mayor." He had read sentences like that a hundred times and never once felt the floor shift under them. Now he felt it. The sentence was doing two jobs at once, reporting the claim and attributing it, and the attribution was the whole story. If the writer had known it as fact, the writer wouldn't have needed the mayor to say it. Spanish news writers used "según," which meant "according to," to mark that a statement came from a source, not from the reporter. Nobody had to tell him this; he could see it working in front of him, the little word standing guard between the claim and the person writing it.

He recorded the summary twice and hated both. On the third try he got it out in one breath: the article was about the plant, that the mayor said it would close by spring, that the company said three hundred jobs, and that according to the paper's sources, nothing had been signed. His accent mangled half of it. He did not care as much as he expected to.

It was only then, with the file saved and sent, that he told them. "My mom works at Bexwell," he said. "The plant in the article. It's the one." The kitchen went quiet enough that he could hear the fridge hum. Angel put her pencil down. Nada, who had known something was wrong since he chose the article, said nothing, which was its own kind of answer.

"You could have said," Angel said.

"Then it would have been a thing. With the whole thing out loud, I'd have been reading it like it was my life ending. I wanted to read it like it was Spanish homework."

"And?"

"And it's the mayor saying it. Según el alcalde. It's his statement. The reporter didn't confirm it. Three hundred jobs is the company's number. Nothing's signed." He heard how it sounded, the way he was holding the grammar up like a shield, and he stopped. "That's what I know. That's all I know. It might still happen."

The doorbell rang, and it was Mr. He from next door, holding a container of soup he'd misdelivered on purpose, the way he did when a house had three bikes in the yard and he wanted an excuse to check on it. Nada's mother let him in and he stood in the doorway of the kitchen, taking in the laptops, the drawing, the boy with the shutdown look on his face.

"Homework on a Saturday," he said. "Brutal."

"Just finished," Chase said.

Mr. He nodded at that, unhurried, and set the soup on the counter. "Well," he said. "Then you've earned some of this."

Chase looked at the container, then at his phone, dark now on the table, the summary already sent, his mother's shift ending in forty minutes.

"Can I borrow a bike?" he said. "I want to get home before she does."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
The folding table in Elijah's grandmother's backyard had been laid with enough food to debilitate a small army: two trays of lasagna, a pot of rice and peas, his aunt's famous macaroni pie, and a cake in the shape of a graduation cap that leaned slightly to one side, like it had already celebrated a little too hard. Elijah sat in the middle of it all in his gown, which he had refused to take off even though the ceremony had ended four hours ago, because, as he told his cousin, "I wore this thing for four years of my life, I'm getting at least one evening out of it."

His grandmother kept reaching over to smooth his collar, which didn't exist, since the gown had no collar. "You look like a professor," she said. "Like a little professor." Elijah let her do it. Somewhere between the third and fourth smoothing, the gate latch clicked and Princess came through carrying a bowl of salad as her admission ticket, with John behind her holding nothing except his phone, which he claimed contained photos of the ceremony he had not actually attended.

"You missed it," Elijah said. "You missed the whole thing."

"I watched the livestream," John said, "for eleven minutes. The valedictorian's elocution was putting me to sleep. She paused after every third word like she was being paid by the pause." He dropped into a chair and stole a piece of plantain. "Also your grandmother just handed me a plate, so technically I'm a guest now."

Princess sat down slowly, the way she did when she was working out how to say something. She had been at the ceremony, near the front, and Elijah had watched her during the principal's speech, watched her mouth tighten at one particular moment. Now she set the salad bowl down and said, "Did you count?"

"Count what?"

"The chairs. On the field." She turned her fork over and over on her plate. "They set out chairs for everyone who started grade nine with us. And I counted the empty ones while they were reading names. I couldn't help it. Some of them read a name and nobody stood up."

The table went quiet in that particular way, where the aunts kept passing food but stopped talking, and the music from the speaker suddenly seemed very loud. Elijah's uncle reached over and turned it down without being asked.

"DeShawn," John said, not a question.

"DeShawn. Marcus. That whole table that used to sit by the vending machines." Princess looked at Elijah. "You know what I mean. You sat with them in grade ten."

Elijah did know. He had spent most of tenth grade at that table, doing homework he wasn't supposed to be helping with, arguing with Marcus about whether algebra was a scam invented to ruin adolescence, before Marcus's family moved and nobody said where, and before DeShawn stopped coming altogether. Elijah had thought about him maybe four times since. That number embarrassed him now, being so precise and so small.

"There's a thing I read," Elijah said, and immediately regretted starting that way, because John mouthed there's a thing I read back at him with theatrical awe. "Shut up. It was for the civics essay. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year." He said it fast, the way he had memorized it, then slowed down. "Adjusted cohort. That means they count everyone who started ninth grade together, and they see how many of that group actually finish. Across the whole country it was 87 percent that year."

"Thirteen percent don't finish," Princess said quietly.

"That's not some other school," Elijah said. "That's our chairs on the field."

Mr. Aydın, who lived two houses down and had apparently smelled the lasagna from a distance diplomatic enough to pretend was a coincidence, had been listening from the end of the table while building an ambitious plate. He set down his fork. "In my class this year," he said, "I had a boy who was the funniest person in the room and the furthest behind. Some days I could not get both of those boys to be the same boy." He shrugged and went back to his lasagna, and nobody at the table knew what to do with that, so they didn't do anything with it, which itself felt like an answer of a kind.

"So what are we saying?" John asked, getting bellicose the way he always did when a conversation turned sad, jabbing his fork toward the cake. "That we should feel guilty for graduating? I refuse to feel guilty for graduating. I worked for this. You worked for this. Princess worked so hard for this she made the rest of us look bad."

"I'm not saying guilty," Elijah said. "I'm saying I don't know what it is. It's not guilty and it's not not guilty." He looked at his gown sleeve, at the stupid shiny polyester of it. "I keep thinking about Marcus arguing algebra was a scam, and how I laughed, and how that was probably his best day of grade ten. And I'm not saying that was my job, to be his reason to stay. I genuinely don't think it was. But I also don't think it was nothing."

The candles on the leaning cake had never been lit, and his grandmother appeared at that moment with a lighter held high like a torch, declaring that the speeches would begin whether the speeches were ready or not. John raised his glass of ginger ale and said, "To the 87 percent," and it came out louder and less joking than he meant it to, so that the whole table, even the aunts who had no idea what he was talking about, raised their glasses too.

Elijah lifted his cup last. He still didn't have the word for what he felt, sitting there in his gown with the empty chairs on the field behind him and his whole noisy family in front, and he decided, holding his cup up into the smoke of the candles, that maybe he wasn't supposed to have it yet.

"To the chairs," he said. "Even the empty ones."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Raphael arrived at the park eleven minutes early, which was a mistake, because eleven minutes gave him time to count everything that could go wrong. He had chosen the bench by the duck pond because it was the only spot in the whole park he actually liked: riparian willows trailing their branches in the green water, an ice cream cart within sight, and enough passing foot traffic that silence would never be total. He straightened the collar of the shirt he had argued about with his mother for twenty minutes, and then unstraightened it, on the theory that a too-neat collar looked desperate.

Trista arrived on a bicycle, braked too late, and skidded slightly on the gravel. "Okay," she said, dropping the bike in the grass, "before you say anything, yes, I know I'm four minutes late, and no, the bike was not the plan. My brother took the car keys hostage."

"It's fine. I've only been here for a week."

"A week?" She sat down on the far end of the bench, which he tried not to interpret as a verdict. "What did you do for a week?"

"Watched ducks. Fed ducks. Lionized ducks, honestly. That one there, with the white collar, I've decided he's a war hero."

She laughed, which he hadn't expected, and the laugh loosened something in his chest. Still, the conversation kept snagging. He talked too much about the physics teacher everyone hated; she talked about her job at the garden centre and he realized, halfway through, that he had interrupted her twice. When they bought ice cream, he dropped a coin under the cart and spent an absurd thirty seconds crawling for it while the cashier waited with the patience of a saint. Trista laughed again, but he could not tell whether it was with him or at the general catastrophe of him.

Gurshan found him there by accident, or claimed it was an accident, wheeling a wagon of recycling he was collecting for the deposit money. Gurshan wanted a ticket to the concert in November the way other people wanted oxygen, and had been collecting bottles for six weeks with a zeal that their classmates had begun to lionize ironically and then, when the bag count rose past four hundred, sincerely. "Is this the date?" he stage-whispered, twenty feet away, with absolutely no discretion. "Are you on the date right now?"

"Keep walking, Gurshan."

"I'm walking. I'm gone." But he wasn't gone; he was orbiting, and eventually Trista waved him over, and the three of them sat arguing about whether the concert was worth four hundred cans, and it was, weirdly, the best part of the afternoon. Trista and Gurshan had known each other since grade five and insulted each other with the fluency of siblings. Raphael mostly listened, and when Trista left, she said, "This was good, Raphael," in a tone so neutral it could have meant anything, and rode off before he composed a reply.

He walked home with Gurshan pulling the wagon, and the replaying began. Every interruption, the dropped coin, the stretch where he'd told the story about the physics teacher and she'd just said "huh." He concluded, with the confidence of a judge, that she had endured the afternoon out of politeness. "She hated it," he said. "You saw her face when I dropped the coin."

"Wait, you think that?" Gurshan stopped the wagon. "Okay, so in psych class we did this thing, a 2018 study by Erica Boothby and her colleagues. They found a liking gap. After a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. That's the whole finding. Everybody walks around thinking it went worse than it did."

"So it's not just me."

"It's the default setting, apparently. You're not special." Gurshan resumed pulling the wagon, the bottles clinking like a wind chime. Raphael turned this over. Part of him wanted to seize it as permission to hope; another part, an older and more suspicious part, noted that Gurshan had gotten a C plus in that class. He did not know if the finding applied to him, to this afternoon, to a girl on a bicycle who said "this was good" like a weather report. That was the honest residue: the gap was real, but so was the not-knowing.

His phone buzzed against his leg. He checked it, half expecting the group chat. It was Trista. Next Saturday, same bench? Bring the war hero duck's biography. Also tell Gurshan the recycling thing is actually amazing.

Raphael read it twice. Gurshan, craning over his shoulder, said, "Tell her four hundred and six cans," with great dignity.

"Four hundred and six," Raphael typed, "and rising." He hit send, pocketed the phone, and helped push the wagon up the hill.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
Sarah had cut the list to seven and could not make it smaller, and Mr. Flores had told her twice that the deadline did not care how she felt about it.

She sat in his classroom after the last bell, the applications spread across two desks she had pushed together. On the left, the brochure for Edinburgh. On the right, a printout from a UCAS page Kelly had found for her, because Sarah had spent a week pretending the system was the same as the American one and had nearly missed it entirely.

"Five," Kelly said, dropping into the chair opposite. "That's it. Five courses, and you list them with no order of preference. It's not like here, where you rank them."

"So they all count the same."

"They all count the same."

Sarah looked at her seven. History at Edinburgh, history at Durham, history at St Andrews, archaeology at Durham, history at York, ancient history at Nottingham, and heritage conservation at a place she had only visited once, in the rain, and had loved without being able to say why.

"Cut two," Kelly said.

"Easy for you. You're staying."

Kelly was going to the state university forty minutes from her house, and she had known since October, and her mother had already bought her a duvet. Sarah's parents had separated the summer before senior year, and the arbitration over the house had gone on so long that it had incapacitated the whole family's ability to make any other decision. That was how Sarah thought of it. The lawyer's letters arrived, and everyone stopped being able to choose anything, from restaurants to colleges, as if choosing were a muscle that had been strained.

"Give me the pen," Kelly said. "I'll cut for you."

"You will not."

Sarah crossed out heritage conservation first, which surprised her, because she had expected it to be hardest. But it was the one she could not defend to anyone, not to her father, who had asked whether it was a job or a hobby, not to the form itself. She wrote it small in the margin of her notebook, though, the full name of the course, so it would still exist somewhere.

"That's one," Kelly said.

"Shut up."

Six left. Mr. Flores came back in from the hallway with his coffee and stood at the board, not helping, which was his way of helping. "When I couldn't decide," he said, "my wife told me to flip a coin, and then notice whether I was hoping for heads while it was in the air."

"That's not a real method," Sarah said.

"It's not. But it's information."

He left again. Sarah looked at archaeology at Durham, which was the course her mother wanted, and at history at St Andrews, which was the course her mother had wanted before the separation, back when they had looked at photographs of the town together on the couch. Her mother still mentioned St Andrews. Her father had never mentioned any of them, but she had once heard him on the phone say he was tired of living out of a suitcase, and she had thought about that for weeks.

She flipped the pen instead of a coin. St Andrews won, and she felt nothing, which she noted, and which unsettled her more than hoping would have.

She cut Nottingham, because the course was the weakest fit, and kept six, and could not get to five, and the clock in the room ticked like it was being paid to.

Melanie came in looking for Mr. Flores's stapler, saw the paper, and said, "Why do you have two at Durham?"

"History and archaeology."

"Same city, two courses. That's your problem right there." Melanie took the stapler and left before Sarah could argue, which was annoying, because Melanie was right in the way people are right when they haven't been thinking about something for a month.

Sarah sat with it. If the five were listed with no order of preference, then the list was not a ranking of her heart; it was a set, a geography, a shape of the person she might be in eighteen months. Two courses at Durham meant she was keeping two versions of herself in one town. She crossed out archaeology. Five. History at Edinburgh, Durham, St Andrews and York, ancient history at Nottingham restored, and, after a long minute with the pen above heritage conservation, that one too, back from the margin, replacing York.

"You just did the opposite of what I'd do," Kelly said.

"I know."

She typed the five into the form. Her mother wanted St Andrews; her father wanted her near enough to visit on a weekend; she wanted the rain-soaked conservation course and could not say why. All five went in beside each other, equal, unordered, and whichever offer came back first would arrive looking no different from the others.

"Done?" Kelly said.

"Done."

She closed the laptop. Outside the window, Mr. Flores was crossing the parking lot with his empty mug, and Melanie was calling something to him from the doorway that Sarah couldn't hear.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: The Truman Doctrine, announced in March 1947, pledged US support for countries resisting communist pressure, starting with aid to Greece and Turkey.
story:
Hunter had the two photocopies side by side on the library table when Farhan dropped his bag onto the third chair and sat down without asking.

"Ms. Sutherland still wants the essay Friday?" Farhan peeled an orange under the table, against the rules, and the smell filled the corner by the biography shelves.

"Friday." Hunter slid one photocopy toward him. "This one says the Americans caused the Cold War. Economic expansion, they needed markets, the Soviets just reacted. The other one says the Soviets caused it, ideology, expansion by nature. Pick."

"I picked my topic already. The space race." Farhan sucked a strip of peel. "Why do you care which one's right?"

That was the problem. Hunter had spent Sunday at his grandfather's house building a timeline on butcher paper, taping index cards along a pencil line, and the two of them had argued for an hour about where to put the first card. His grandfather, sanguine about most things, had not been sanguine about that. He had rapped his knuckle on a card with a speech on it, a single date in the corner, and said that was the hinge, everything after was reaction. Hunter had thought the earlier document mattered more, the long, pessimistic analysis from Moscow, and he had said so, and his grandfather had gone quiet in the way that meant the argument was not about history anymore.

In the library now, he looked up the speech itself. He found it in an anthology of postwar documents and read the page twice, then copied the citation onto an index card. March 1947: the president had pledged support for countries resisting communist pressure, and the aid was to go first to Greece and Turkey. He wrote the two countries down and underlined them, then stopped underlining because it looked like the beginnings of an answer he had not earned yet.

"So the money went to Greece and Turkey," Abigaelle said, reading over his shoulder. She had arrived at some point with a stack of books about marine biology and claimed the other end of the table as hers. "That's the Truman Doctrine, right? My brother did it last year."

"That's it." Hunter laid the card on his timeline draft, then placed the Moscow document's date to its left. "Okay. Expansion-by-nature guy says the doctrine proves the Americans were imperial, money and bases, Greece and Turkey guarding the Mediterranean. Market guy says it was defensive, look at what the Soviets were doing first, the Americans were reacting."

"Both of them use the same speech?"

"Both of them use the same speech."

Farhan leaned over, orange still in one hand. "So it can't prove both. Evidence doesn't work like that."

Abigaelle pulled one of her marine biology books closer, but she kept watching them. Hunter stacked the two historians' essays and squared the edges. Farhan was right, and it was worse than Farhan knew: if the same March 1947 pledge could anchor two opposite stories, then the evidence was not going to settle anything by itself. You had to weigh the interpretations, and weighing meant deciding what would count against each one. He turned the expansion essay over and wrote on the back, in small letters, what would have to be true for the market argument to fail. Then he did the same for the other. Both lists looked short and unsatisfying. The historiography unit had warned about this, the way arguments atrophy into reflexes when you stop testing them, and he had thought that was a phrase for other people, the kind of polymath who read footnotes for fun, whoever that was. Now he was the one on his third page of scribbled tests.

The library clock moved toward closing. Farhan had drifted to the computers, and Abigaelle was copying diagrams of gills. Hunter lined up his cards along the table's edge like his grandfather's butcher paper: the pessimistic analysis from Moscow, then the March 1947 pledge, then Greece and Turkey, then everything after. He moved the first card forward, then back, then forward again. Somewhere on the drive home he would have to tell his grandfather where he had put the hinge, and he did not yet know what he would say, only that he would say it with the two lists in his pocket and the dates exactly right. He picked up the Greece and Turkey card, held it against the light, and set it down half a card's width later than before.

"Better?" Abigaelle asked, not looking up.

"I'll know when he argues with me."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
Nobody in Room 214 knew that Alexis had not read past chapter ten of Pride and Prejudice, and she intended to keep it that way. She had read the SparkNotes on the bus, twice, and she had read the first section of a different book entirely, the one her mother kept by the toaster, which is why, when Ms. Sow asked them to bring "a critical lens" to Thursday's book club, Alexis raised her hand and said she had one.

"A Marxist lens," she said. "From the Communist Manifesto. Marx and Engels, 1848. The first section opens by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles."

Ms. Sow looked at her for a long moment, the way she looked at vending machines that ate quarters. "Well," she said. "That's more than most of you brought."

There were five of them at the table by the window: Alexis, Leticia, Bianka, a boy whose name Alexis deliberately never learned, and Ms. Sow, who ran the club for a honorarium of forty dollars a semester, paid by the parent association, though she said she would do it for free and everyone believed she said that about everything. The radiator ticked. Outside, the parking lot was turning orange with October light.

"Okay," said Leticia, turning her battered paperback over. "So does it fit? Is Pride and Prejudice about class struggle?"

"Obviously," said Bianka, before Alexis could speak. "The whole book is about money. Mrs. Bennet says it in chapter one, basically. If Mr. Bennet dies they lose the house, so the girls have to marry rich. That's not romance, that's economics."

"Then why do we read it as romance?" the boy asked.

"That's the question," said Ms. Sow, and leaned back, and said nothing more, which Alexis understood to be a trap.

Here is what Alexis had not told anyone, including herself, in any deliberate way: she had picked the Manifesto not because she believed it but because her older cousin had left it at their apartment in June, and her father had swept it into a drawer with the junk mail, and Alexis had taken it out and read the first page on the bus, and something about the rhythm of it had made her sit up straighter. She had told Leticia she was "into theory." That was a lie shaped like a truth. She was into the feeling of reading it, which is not the same thing, and she did not yet know the difference.

"Alexis?" said Ms. Sow. "You brought the lens. Apply it."

Alexis looked down at the passage Ms. Sow had photocopied, the one from chapter fifty-six, Lady Catherine confronting Elizabeth about Darcy. She had not read this chapter. The words were strange to her, all of them, and the margins of the photocopy were as blank as the parking lot. She felt the silence begin to metastasize around the table, spreading from face to face, Leticia's eyebrows going up, Bianka turning her pen over and over.

"Elizabeth refuses her," Alexis said slowly, because that much had been in the SparkNotes. "Lady Catherine tells her she's nobody, and Elizabeth says her refusal is her answer anyway." She paused. Something was assembling itself, the way a photograph develops. "But Lady Catherine isn't just being cruel. She's defending a line. If Elizabeth marries Darcy, the line stops meaning anything. So the struggle isn't a sword fight, it's a drawing room. It's still a struggle."

"Say more," said Ms. Sow, but gently, and Alexis understood that she had been caught, though not in the way she'd feared.

From the window seat, Leticia watched Alexis's face do something she had never seen it do, which was think without performing. Leticia had known Alexis since seventh grade, had watched her win every argument she ever entered, and had privately concluded that Alexis's opinions were like her eyeliner, applied in the bathroom mirror in four minutes and flawless. But this was different. Alexis had her finger on the photocopy and her eyes were somewhere past the wall.

"It's just," Alexis was saying, "I don't know if I believe the Manifesto fits. I mean, Marx and Engels say it's all hitherto existing society. All of it. But Elizabeth isn't trying to overthrow the class that's crushing her. She's trying to marry into it. She wins by joining. Isn't that the opposite of struggle? Or is that the cleverest kind, the kind where nobody admits it's a fight?"

"That's the whole thing," Bianka said, quiet. "That's why Mrs. Bennet is a joke in the book and she shouldn't be. She's the only one who sees the truth and everyone laughs at her for it."

"That's gratuitous, honestly," Leticia said. "Austen punishing the character who understands the economy."

The radiator ticked. The boy said, "So the book is either proof of the Manifesto or proof it's wrong, and we can't tell which," and Ms. Sow smiled at the ceiling as if it owed her money.

The bell rang before anyone resolved anything, which Alexis suspected was Ms. Sow's plan all along. In the hall, Leticia caught her arm. "You lied about reading the book," she said. Alexis said nothing. "It's fine. Whatever happened at that table, it wasn't a lie." Alexis zipped her bag over the borrowed Manifesto, the cousin's copy with the cracked spine, and stood there holding it against her chest.

"I'm going to finish it this time," she said. "Both of them."

"Which first?"

Alexis looked down the crowded hallway, at all those girls walking toward the buses and the future their mothers had planned, and said, "The one where somebody gets the house."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: In a standard repayment mortgage, early monthly payments go mostly toward interest, and later payments go mostly toward paying down the amount borrowed.
story:
The listing said eleven o'clock sharp, and Jonathan's mother had them there at ten fifty, standing on the pavement outside a brick building with a buzzer panel and a row of mailboxes streaked with old rain. She kept smoothing the front of her coat as though it might say something first. Jonathan held the folded printout of the advertisement, mostly for something to do with his hands, because the truth was he would rather have been anywhere else, and the ennui of trailing his mother through other people's apartments had become, over the past month, a familiar weight, like a stone in his pocket.

A woman came down the steps jangling keys. "Ms. Sokolov," she said. "You're the ten o'clock, the Henderson viewing?" She was already turning the lock on the front door, so they followed her up a staircase that smelled faintly of someone else's cooking. "First month's rent and a deposit, that's the standard here. Deposit's five weeks, held in a protection scheme, not my pocket, mind."

"Five weeks," Jonathan's mother repeated, as if tasting it.

"Plus the month up front. You'll want references, naturally." Ms. Sokolov pushed open the door of 3B and stood aside to let them past.

Inside, the rooms were emptier than Jonathan had expected, the previous tenants gone so recently that the curtains still hung. He drifted to the window while his mother asked about council tax and the boiler, and it was there, looking down at the car park, that he saw Kallie from his form coming up the path with a younger woman carrying a baby on her hip.

They met on the landing a minute later. "Oh, it's you," Kallie said, surprised into something almost like pleasure. "This is my cousin. She's buying, but she wanted to see what the rents are doing round here." The cousin nodded a greeting and went in to find Ms. Sokolov, and Kallie lingered with Jonathan on the worn carpet.

"Buying," Jonathan said. "How does anyone our age's family do that?"

" hers didn't." Kallie shrugged. "You should hear her on it. She's had the house five years and she says the payments barely touched what she owes. She showed me the statement. Five years of paying, every month, on time, and the balance went down this much." He held up a thumb and finger, nearly touching. "I thought that was insane. I asked her where the money was going."

"Where?"

"Interest, she says. On a repayment mortgage the early payments mostly go on the interest, and it's only later, way down the line, the payments mostly go on actually paying down what you borrowed. So she's been paying for five years and basically still owes for the house." Kallie said it flatly, the way people repeat things they can't fix. "She calls it pernicious. Big word for a Tuesday."

Jonathan looked through the doorway at his mother, who was standing in the empty kitchen holding a leaflet about the deposit scheme, her thumb moving along the figures as though checking them for a second time.

"Who's that envelope for?" Kallie asked quietly. He hadn't realised she'd seen it, the brown envelope his mother had kept switching between coat pockets all morning. He hadn't seen inside it either. He had assumed it was the deposit, the first month, the money that made this day possible, the way you assume the floor is where it was yesterday.

"I don't know," he said, and found that it was true.

His mother came out to the landing to ask Ms. Sokolov something about the notice period, and while the two women talked by the door, Jonathan did what he had been avoiding for a month: he thought about the house they had left, the one with the roses his mother had planted the spring everything seemed fine. He had come home one day and the furniture was going, and there had been a word, said quietly on the phone at night, a word he now recognised everywhere: mortgage. He had thought a mortgage was like a rent that ended, a long slow buying. Kallie's cousin had paid five years and owed almost the whole thing still. His mother had paid eleven.

"You're quiet," his mother said, coming back.

He could have asked her then, right there on the landing, what the envelope held, whether it was a deposit for a future or the last of something past, whether the payments had gone the way Kallie described, into interest, into the years, into nothing that could be shown for it. He wanted to forestall the question she might ask him first, the cheerful one about whether he liked the room, whether he could see himself here. Instead he said, "The small room's fine. The light's good in the morning."

Her face changed, some tightness going out of it, and she squeezed the envelope once in her pocket, a small private motion, like a heartbeat.

"So," Ms. Sokolov called from the doorway, keys already in hand, "shall we say you'd like to take it?"

His mother looked at Jonathan, and the envelope crackled faintly under her fingers.

"Can I see what's in it?" he asked.

She looked down at her coat, then at him, and after a moment drew it out and held it out flat on her palm, unsealed.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Tinker v. Des Moines (1969), the Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate.
story:
The kettle on her grandmother's stove had a habit of sighing before it whistled, and Emily had learned to wait for the sigh. She spread her notes across the kitchen table, which was really the table where her grandfather had once spread seed catalogs, and tried to imagine it was a bench. Two days from now she would stand in the mock courtroom at school and argue a case about a girl suspended for wearing a T-shirt, and Mr. Hussain, who coached the team and assigned the sides, had given her the strangest instruction of her two years on it. She would argue for the school first, then for the student, in the same afternoon.

"Both sides," Abigail said from the doorway, two grocery bags in her arms. "He actually wants you to argue against yourself."

"He wants me to find out which one I believe," Emily said, though she wasn't sure that was true. It might be that he wanted her to find out that she couldn't decide, which seemed like a crueler assignment.

Omar arrived ten minutes later with his laptop under his arm and the confident air of someone who had already finished his own brief, which he had not. He settled into the chair by the window, where the afternoon light came off the river, and opened a document that contained three sentences and a list of snacks he intended to buy. Emily slid her folder across to him.

"Here's my problem," she said. "When I argue for the school, I keep sounding like a censor. When I argue for the student, I keep sounding naive. Somewhere in the middle there's a thing I can't see yet."

"The middle is usually where the law lives," Omar said, typing something that was probably the word "middle" and nothing else. "Or where it hides. Depends on your metaphysics."

"Do not say metaphysics in a brief," Abigail said. She had found the kettle and was watching it with the patience of someone who had also learned to listen for the sigh. "You'll sound like a philosophy major."

"I am going to be a philosophy major," Omar said, mildly wounded.

Emily turned her chair toward the window. Below the garden, past the flat stones her grandmother called the landing, the river moved in its unhurried way, and along its bank grew the ragged line of willows and alders that her grandfather had tended because, he said once, a man who owns riparian land owes the water something. She had written that down when she was twelve, not understanding it, and only lately had begun to. What did the water want from the bank? What did the bank owe back? She caught herself wondering whether a school and its students stood in anything like that relation, and then caught herself again, because a metaphor was not an argument, and Mr. Hussain would say so.

She read her strongest paragraph aloud, the one for the school, about order and the vulnerability of classrooms, and Abigail winced at the exact sentence Emily had privately winced at. Then she read the paragraph for the student, and Omar said it swung too far, that it treated a hallway as a public square, which no court had ever quite done. He tapped at his keyboard, frowning, and turned the screen toward her.

"This might be your thing you can't see," he said. "Tinker v. Des Moines, 1969. The Supreme Court ruled seven to two that students do not shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech at the schoolhouse gate."

Emily read it twice. The line had a shape she recognized, the shape of something people quoted when they wanted the argument to be over. Students do not shed their rights, she thought; therefore the school loses, therefore her T-shirt paragraph was doomed. She said as much, and Abigail, pouring the water over the teabags, shook her head.

"Seven to two," Abigail said. "Not nine to nothing. Two people looked at the same hallway and saw something different."

Emily sat with that. She pulled a clean sheet toward her and, without deciding which side she was drafting for, began to write. If the right did not stop at the gate, then the question was not whether the student had it but what it could carry through the gate with it, what a right weighed against forty other students trying to learn. She wrote a sentence about the boundary being real but permeable, like the bank of a river, which was the water's and the land's at once, and she left the image in because for once it was doing the work of an idea rather than decorating one. Then, underneath, she wrote the counterargument she would have to face when she switched sides: that the school could always claim disruption, and that a right which dissolved whenever an administrator used that word was not much of a right. Both sentences felt true. She could not make them sit still together.

They worked until the light moved off the river and onto the ceiling. Omar drafted questions for cross-examination, and Abigail, who had given up pretending to be neutral, read the student side aloud in the voice of someone enjoying herself. When Emily's grandmother came in from the garden with tomatoes, she listened to half a sentence about the schoolhouse gate, nodded as though the Supreme Court were a neighbor she had opinions about, and went back out.

Near dusk, Mr. Hussain's reply to Emily's earlier email arrived, and she read it standing by the window. He had written only three lines. The first praised her framing. The second asked what she would do if the judges asked her, flat out, which side she believed. The third said that a good advocate can hold a position and still know where it is thin.

"So which do you believe?" Omar asked, watching her face.

"I believe the gate is real," Emily said slowly, "and I believe rights don't stop at it, and I have not yet found the sentence where both of those things are true at once."

"Maybe there isn't one," Abigail said.

"Maybe there isn't one," Emily agreed, and she sat back down, and drew a line under both sentences, and wrote beneath the line: find out Thursday.

The kettle sighed.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: In The Two Fridas, one Frida wears a white European-style Victorian dress and the other wears a traditional Tehuana dress, a contrast often read as her mixed European and Mexican heritage.
story:
Owen had promised himself he would not say anything stupid in the art room today, which was a maxim he'd already broken twice by the time Ms. Abdi set the print on the easel. The painting showed two women seated side by side, holding hands, and each of them was Frida Kahlo. One wore a white European-style Victorian dress with buttons up the front, delicate and buttoned to the throat. The other wore a traditional Tehuana dress, bright and embroidered, the kind of garment Owen had seen in photographs of Mexican festivals. Both women exposed a heart, and a single vein joined the two hearts like a thread between spools.

"Formal analysis," Ms. Abdi said, tapping the easel. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Not whether you like it. Whether you can say what it does."

Matt leaned over the table, squinting. "Okay, but which one is the real Frida?"

Tania didn't even look up from her notebook. "The one on the right. Obviously. The Tehuana dress is who she actually is. The white one is like, a costume."

"That's backwards," Matt said. "The Victorian dress is European, and her dad was European, so that's half of her. You can't just pick the half you like better."

"You can if the painting does."

Owen watched the two of them argue and felt the argument go somewhere the painting didn't quite go. His assignment sheet sat in front of him with three headings: colour, composition, symbolism, and he had written nothing under any of them. He had a garrulous inner voice that wanted to fill the page with opinions, and he had a suspicion that the assignment was asking for something harder, something quieter. He tried to predicate his reading on what he could actually see, starting with the colours. The sky behind the women was turbulent, grey and bruised. The Victorian dress was white but almost glowing against it. The Tehuana dress carried golds and blues, and there was a small portrait held in one Frida's hand, which the vein ran toward, as if the whole painting's blood circled through that tiny picture.

"Composition," he said aloud, mostly to himself, but the room was small and both of them heard.

"Go on," Ms. Abdi said. She had a way of saying it that made it not optional.

"They're the same size," Owen said. "Same chair height, same face almost. The painting doesn't rank them. If one were smaller, or turned away, I'd pick the other as real. But it's, like, symmetrical. They're holding hands and they share the blood." He hesitated, because the next part felt risky. "Maybe the question isn't which one is real. Maybe the contrast is the point. One dress European, one dress Mexican, and she painted them both because she was both."

Tania sat back. "You're saying we're asking a question the painting already answered?"

"I'm saying it might not be a question. Or the answer is both, or neither, and I can't fully tell which, and I think that's allowed."

Matt pointed at the exposed hearts, one whole, one cut and bleeding. "One's bleeding though. That one's dying, isn't it? That has to mean something."

"It means something," Owen agreed. "I just don't know what yet, and I'd rather say that than make it up." Tania laughed, and for once it didn't sound like she was laughing at him, more like she was surprised.

They worked for another ten minutes, trading observations, and Owen filled in his headings with things he could defend: the shared horizon line, the way the vein behaved like a compositional element, the little portrait as a symbolic anchor. He still had a blank line under symbolism where the hearts went, and he wrote "uncertain" beside it and did not cross it out.

Then came the twist, or what felt like one. Ms. Abdi walked past his table, glanced at his sheet, and stopped. "Owen. This painting is a self-portrait." She let that sit for a second while he absorbed it, both women, one artist, one body of work staring out of two faces. "So when you ask which is real," she said, gathering the prints from the other tables, "you're asking a woman to draw herself and then cut herself in half and hand you the scissors."

Owen looked back at the two Fridas holding hands, and under his blank line he wrote a small question mark, then drew, without thinking, a line connecting it to his name at the top of the page.

"That's going to look weird when I grade it," Ms. Abdi said.

"It's my vein," Owen said, and Tania snorted so hard she knocked over the water cup.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769, using knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain.
story:
Emily had spread the ocean current map across the picnic table like a tablecloth for a very damp dinner party, and Noam was already poking at it. "Why is the Atlantic wearing a scarf," he said, tracing the red ribbon that curled up the coast and pointed its nose toward Europe.

"Because it's warm and it's showing off," Emily said. She smoothed a wrinkle with the heel of her hand. The assignment was Ms. Vogel's: explain, by Friday, how the Gulf Stream keeps northern Europe warmer than it has any right to be. Emily had assumed it would be a paragraph. It had turned into three library books, two arguments with Matthias, and now this, the map, pinned to the table by ketchup bottles because she'd forgotten the clothespins.

Matthias arrived through the gap in the fence carrying his little sister's blow-up globe under one arm, deflated, like a sad orange. "Auxiliary visual aid," he announced. "Don't ask how I got it."

"You're not blowing that up here," Emily said.

"It's already got a hole. Look, it undulates when I wave it." He waved it and it did, sadly, like a jellyfish waving goodbye. He sat down, folded it into his lap, and frowned at the map. "Okay, so the water goes north. Why does that make London not frozen? Scotland grows palm trees, I looked it up, actual palm trees on the coast."

"Ireland has palm trees too," Noam said. "I feel like that's a trick of some kind."

"It's not a trick, it's water." Emily pulled the second book toward her, the old one with the reproduction plates. She'd found it Tuesday, hunting for something else entirely, and had sat in the aisle for twenty minutes with her mouth slightly open. "You two, guess how people first figured out where the Gulf Stream was. No satellites, no sensors, no anything."

"Fishermen noticed the water was warm," Matthias said.

"Better than that." She turned the book around. The plate showed the Atlantic with a long hatched band drawn across it, annotated in cramped eighteenth-century lettering. "Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769. Look at this thing. It's gorgeous. And the reason he could draw it, the whole reason, was his cousin, Timothy Folger. A Nantucket whaling captain. Franklin asked him how the current worked, and Folger just knew, because the whalemen had been reading the water their whole lives."

"Wait." Noam leaned in. "So ship captains were saving days by avoiding the current before anyone had a name for it on paper?"

"Way before satellites. Decades and decades. The packet ships were fighting the current and losing, and the whalers knew to steer around it, and nobody had told the mail captains because nobody thought to ask." She tapped the plate. "Folger drew it out for him. That's this. This exact hatchwork is a whaleman's knowledge wearing a scientist's suit."

Matthias was quiet for a second, which for Matthias was practically a speech. Then he said, "Okay but that's weird, right? Franklin's the famous one. The chart says Franklin. Folger's a footnote in his own ocean."

"That's the part I keep chewing on." Emily sat back. The ketchup bottles held the map's corners down; the red river ran on regardless, toward Iceland, toward Norway, toward palm trees it had never seen. "Because Ms. Vogel wants us to explain the mechanism, the water, the heat, all of that. And I can do that part now, mostly. But the thing that actually grabbed me is how the knowing happened. Two different kinds of knowing, folded together. Franklin couldn't feel the current. Folger couldn't print it."

"So which one is your Friday answer?" Noam asked. "The water or the cousins?"

"That's the fight I'm having with myself, thanks for joining." Emily laughed, but she meant it. She'd drafted two openings on the bus and hated both. One was all isotherms and latitudes, correct and dead. The other was all Folger and the whalemen, alive and hand-wavy. She looked at the map again, the red band undulating north and east, and thought it was like a sentence that needed both its grammar and its voice, the syntax of the current and the people who could read it out loud.

The screen door banged and Ms. Vogel came down her own back steps on the other side of the fence with a watering can, peering over at their arrangement of ketchup bottles and sad globe. "That's a Franklin chart," she called.

"It's a Folger chart with Franklin's name on it," Emily called back, and Ms. Vogel laughed, a short surprised bark, and went on watering her tomatoes.

Matthias blew up the orange globe anyway, in slow purple-faced installments, and when it was half full he set it on the table so the Atlantic faced them, lopsided and bulging. Noam spun it with one finger until the whole ocean wheeled past, the red current on the flat map and the round blue water on the globe showing the same story twice. "Okay," Matthias said, still slightly breathless. "Tell us the Friday version. The one with both of them in it."

Emily put her hand flat on the map, palm covering the hatched band where a whaling captain's knowledge crossed an ocean to get itself printed. "Start like this," she said. "In 1769, London."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, 'this.name = name' uses the keyword 'this' to mean the object's own field when a parameter has the same name.
story:
The camp's demo session started at four o'clock, and by two-thirty Layla's screen still showed the same red text it had shown at noon. She was building a Book class in Java, private fields and getter methods, the way the project sheet demanded, and a tiny test class that should have printed a title and a price. Instead the test printed null and 0.0, every time, with a patience that felt like mockery.

"You're staring at it like it's going to apologize," Lauryn said, sliding into the chair beside her with her own laptop balanced on one arm. Lauryn had finished her project yesterday and had spent the morning teaching a nine-year-old at the other end of the lab how to make a turtle draw a square, which was either generosity or a way of avoiding the volleyball game, or both.

"It assigned nothing," Layla said. "I set the title in the constructor. I know I did. Watch." She ran the test again, and again the console offered null, unperturbed. She opened her notebook, where she had transcribed the instructor's example code line by line during the morning lecture, and set it beside her screen. The two versions looked identical to her. She compared them a second time, character by character, and they still looked identical, which meant her eyes were lying or the machine was.

"Show me your constructor," Lauryn said, and leaned in. Lauryn read slowly, the way she read everything, mouthing slightly. "Okay. Here. Your field is called name, right? Private String name. And your parameter is also name."

"So? That's what the example did."

"Look at the example line. Look at yours."

Layla looked. The example read this.name = name. Hers read name = name. She had copied it in a hurry during the lecture, skipping the small word because it seemed decorative, a verbal tic the instructor had a habit of. She sat back. "That can't matter."

"Run it," Lauryn said, and nudged the laptop toward her.

Layla changed the one line, added the word this in front of the first name, and ran the test. The console printed The Night Circus and 9.99 and Layla made a sound she was slightly embarrassed by, a short whoop that turned the head of Ms. Eze at the front of the room.

"Success?" Ms. Eze asked, without coming over. She had a rule about not hovering during project hours; she said debugging belonged to the person at the keyboard, and she enforced it with a firmness that some campers, privately, called a dysphemism behind her back, though Layla had started to suspect it was just respect wearing a stern face.

"It prints now," Layla called back. "But I don't get why."

"Good," Ms. Eze said. "Tell us at four."

Layla turned to Lauryn instead. "So it's the this. When the parameter has the same name as the field, this.name means the object's own field. That's all the word is doing. It's pointing."

"Parsimonious," Lauryn said with approval. "One keyword, one job. Unlike your notebook, which has three pages on the turtle."

Vivian appeared behind them with four minutes of the break left, holding a plate of watermelon slices from the dining hall, and set one on the desk beside Layla's mouse without comment, because Vivian believed snacks arrived where they were needed and conversation about it only delayed eating. She peered at the screen. "Is that the bug? Vivian's demo is at four-oh-five and she is not ready."

"Vivian is third-person about her panic," Lauryn observed.

"Vivian finds it clarifying." But she was already pulling out her own laptop, and when she opened her constructor Layla saw the same line, name = name, sitting there in Vivian's file like a small closed door. Layla reached over and tapped the screen once, above the line.

"Same one," she said. "Watch." She typed the change, the word this in front of the field, and let Vivian run her own test. It printed. Vivian exhaled through her teeth and ate the watermelon down to the rind.

At four they dragged their chairs into the demo circle. Vivian went first and her test ran clean, and she announced the word this out loud to the room, one keyword, one job, as if she had discovered it in the wild. When Layla's turn came she ran hers, and then stood there for a second with the console glowing behind her, null finally gone, and understood that she could say she'd found the bug all along, or she could say what had actually happened, that she'd copied carelessly and a friend had caught the difference and she'd worked out the rest on her own. She chose the second, mostly, though she left out the whoop.

Outside the lab windows the volleyball game was breaking up, and Lauryn was already gathering her sandals. "Tomorrow," she said, "we transcribe the whole lecture properly. Word by word. Even the boring words."

"Even the boring ones," Layla said, and closed her laptop over the little green checkmark still showing at the bottom of the screen.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
Elijah found the pharmacy receipt first, folded into his father's jacket pocket when he was hauling laundry downstairs. Two numbers were printed at the bottom, circled in ballpoint: 152 over 96, and beside them a single word in his father's cramped handwriting, "again." His father had been to the clinic that afternoon and had said nothing about it at dinner, which meant either it was nothing or it was something, and with his father those were the same silence.

He looked the numbers up on his phone at the kitchen table and felt the evening transfigure around him, the ordinary clutter of mugs and homework becoming the set of a different, more serious play. High. But the sites disagreed about what came next, and one page mentioned that readings taken in clinics could run high for some people, especially people who hated clinics, people like his father, who once admitted he'd rather let a tooth ache for a month than sit in a waiting room. The page used a term, but it dropped off before the explanation loaded, and the wifi in the kitchen had always been unreliable, a subterranean complaint Elijah filed away with the others.

He walked two houses down to Ms. Harper's, because she had been a nurse for thirty years and because she answered her door before he finished knocking. "I need to learn how to take a blood pressure," he said, and heard how it came out, like he was announcing a career. She only said, "Come in, then," and fetched a cuff from a drawer that also held crossword books and a spare pair of reading glasses.

She wrapped the cuff around his own arm first, told him to sit still and stop apologizing, and talked him through the display. Systolic, the top number, when the heart pushed. Diastolic, the bottom, when it rested. She made him take his own reading twice, then take hers, then take his again, and wrote the numbers on the back of an envelope so he could watch them move. "It's a measurement, not a verdict," she said. "It moves all day. That's not a flaw, that's the point."

At school the next day he was distracted through most of lunch while Leighton, their grade's resident raconteur, reenacted a Saturday detention involving a fire door and a vice principal. Alden noticed Elijah scrolling under the table. "What are you actually doing?" Alden asked, and Elijah, surprising himself, put the phone face up and told them both: the receipt, the numbers, the cuff he'd borrowed from Ms. Harper, the term he'd half-read and lost. "White coat," Alden said slowly. "My gran has that. The doctor says her numbers at the office are nothing like her numbers at home." Elijah wrote the phrase down and later, at his desk, found it whole: white coat hypertension, when a reading came out high in a clinic, often from nerves, but normal at home, which was why doctors sometimes checked with readings taken at home or monitored across a whole day before deciding anything. He read it three times. His father was afraid of doctors the way other people were afraid of heights.

That night his father came home late, and Elijah set the cuff on the counter between the toaster and the fruit bowl and said, "Sit down for a minute." His father looked at the cuff, then at him, and something in his face went still. "I know about the reading," Elijah said. "I looked it up. It can read high at the office just because you're tense there, and read normal at home, and doctors check that with home readings or something you wear all day. Before they say anything." His father sat down eventually, unbuttoned his sleeve, and said nothing, which was how he said yes.

The first reading was 138 over 88. The second, after his father had complained about the cuff's grip for a full minute and the complaining had loosened something in him, was 131 over 84. Elijah wrote both numbers in the notebook he'd started, with a column for the time. Over the next week they took readings in the evenings, and he read too about salt, and walking, and how regular exercise seemed to nudge the numbers down over months, and he mentioned the salt at dinner without making a speech about it, just moved the shaker a foot further from his father's elbow and let it sit there.

He knew, if he was honest, that he didn't know yet. He had evenings and a kitchen table, not a clinic, not a whole day of monitoring, and he had no way to say whether the numbers climbing in his notebook were the office, the salt, the walks by the river they'd started taking, or something quieter underneath all of it. He had a page of numbers and a guess. When his father picked up the notebook on Sunday and turned its pages without speaking, Elijah watched him and waited. His father set it down, open to the last entry, and said, "Same time tomorrow," and reached to roll up his sleeve.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
Jack had planned to bowl, because bowling gave a girl something to look at besides his face, but when Priya Unnamed's shift at the pizza place ran late, they ended up at the coffee counter by the shoe rental instead, sharing a table the size of a checkerboard, and after fifteen minutes the conversation had gone quiet in a way that felt like a gutter on the first ball. He had learned that she preferred Diet Coke to coffee, that she'd moved here in eighth grade, and that she thought the bowling alley smelled like "clean feet, if that's a thing." Then nothing. She stirred her drink. He heard a ball rumble down lane six, the clatter of pins, someone's uncle yelling "Yes!" with too much force.

He tried small talk, the way his mother had coached him in the car. School starting soon, the heat, whether the arcade version of air hockey was rigged. Priya answered each one politely, in sentences that got shorter, and Jack felt the evening settling into something polite too, which was worse than awkward, because polite meant it would end at nine and never be repeated.

"Okay," Priya said finally, setting down her straw. "I read about this thing. If we keep doing this, we're both going to go home and forget tonight happened." She pulled out her phone. "There's this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal as they went, and after, the pairs who did the questions felt closer than the pairs who just made small talk." She looked up, half daring him. "We're not strangers exactly, but we're not not strangers. Want to try? We don't have to do all thirty-six."

Jack said yes before he had thought about it, which was its own kind of answer. The first questions were easy, almost stupid: given the choice of anyone in the world, whom would you want as a dinner guest. Priya said her grandmother, who had died before Priya learned enough Farsi to talk to her properly. Jack said a meteorologist, because he wanted to know whether predicting weather felt like magic or like losing slowly, and Priya laughed for the first time in an hour, a real laugh with her whole face.

Somewhere around question twelve, about whether fame would change anything, Jack noticed they had stopped performing. His answers had been jokes at the start, armored jokes, and now he was saying that he secretly believed in a soft kind of determinism, that most of what he'd done was a response to things that had happened to him, and that he found that both comforting and a little humiliating. Priya said, "That's the saddest optimistic thing I've ever heard," and he couldn't tell if she was teasing, which destabilized him pleasantly, the way a lane bumpers shaking a ball toward the pins could still count as a strike.

When they got to question eighteen, the one about what friendship meant to each of them, a woman behind the counter called last call for the grill. Priya's phone buzzed; her ride was outside. They stood in the doorway between the coffee counter and the lanes, under a flickering fluorescent, and Priya said, "We got through eighteen. We skipped the ones about death." Jack said, "We skipped the ones about love too," and then heard himself and felt his ears go hot, because that had sounded like an opening for a speech, and he hadn't meant to make a speech, he'd meant only to be accurate.

He thought about Yash and Anton, who had both given him advice that afternoon in Anton's garage, advice that canceled out. Yash had said be yourself, which was useless, since himself was currently the problem. Anton had said be smooth, which was worse. Standing in the doorway, Jack understood that both of them were half right and that the study was half right too, that the questions hadn't created anything, they had just removed the noise, like gutter bumpers, like a lane swept clean, and what rolled down it was still whatever ball you had brought. He could not say whether what he felt was an incipient something or just the caffeine and the relief of not having to be smooth. He decided he was allowed not to know that yet.

"So," Priya said, pulling her jacket closed. "Nineteen through thirty-six. That's a lot of questions left over."

"Enough for two more dates," Jack said. "If you want to do the math on it."

Priya smiled at the floor, then at him, and pushed open the door into the warm dark of the parking lot. "Text me number nineteen before I get home," she said, and walked toward the waiting headlights.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: Hokusai's print series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, actually contains 46 prints, because ten were added after the first 36 sold well.
story:
The porch boards at her grandmother's house still held the morning's damp when Brooklyn spread all fourteen studies across them, weighted at the corners with teacups and smooth stones from the flowerbed. Ms. Karimi had been clear in May: a portfolio of ten works, unified by a single theme, with an artist's statement to hold it together. Ten. Brooklyn counted again, as if the teacups might have multiplied in the night.

The theme was easy, almost embarrassingly so. Everything she had made since spring circled the same subject: the water tower at the end of her street, drawn from eleven different windows, in rain, in the flat light of February, once at night with a flashlight held under the page. What she couldn't do was choose which drawings to kill. She had come to the house where her grandmother kept the good tracing paper and a drafting table older than her mother, hoping distance would make the choice obvious. Instead she kept lifting pages and setting them back.

Kinsley arrived on her bike before noon, helmet still buckled, and stood over the spread with her hands clasped behind her back like a museum guard. "You know what your problem is," Kinsley said. "You like all of them."

"They're not all good."

"That's not the same thing as cutting them." Kinsley crouched, pulled the night drawing forward, and held it beside one of the rain studies. "These two are the same tower and different worlds. How do you even rank that?"

Brooklyn had tried ranking. She had tried the teacher's method, choosing the ten that best served the statement, and then her own method, keeping the ten she couldn't bear to lose, and the two lists overlapped in only seven places. Somewhere between the lists, she suspected, was her actual portfolio, but she couldn't see it yet. She flipped through the book her grandmother had left on the drafting table, a fat volume of Japanese prints she'd been paging through since she was small, mostly for the waves.

Kurt came by after his shift, smelling of the coffee shop, and read over her shoulder while she stopped on the famous one, the wave with claws and the little boats and the mountain far off in the frame. "That's the one everybody knows," he said.

"It's part of a series." She turned to the copyright page, then back, counting plates with her fingertip because a number she'd half-remembered didn't seem possible. "Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, made around 1830 to 1832, and it actually contains 46 prints." She looked up. "The first 36 sold well, so ten were added after."

Kinsley unbuckled her helmet at last. "So the title is wrong?"

"The title is true and the number is bigger. Both." Brooklyn laughed, surprising herself. She had been treating ten like an ordinance, something posted on a wall that she'd violate at her own peril, rather than what it probably was: a shape to think inside. Even the reticent mountain in the prints, the one that stood back in nearly every image, kept outgrowing the frames people tried to put around it. She wondered whether Ms. Karimi had ever mentioned this on purpose. Probably not. Probably it was just a fact sitting in a book, waiting.

She pulled a notebook from her bag and wrote the statement in the version she'd been avoiding: these are ten views of one tower, and the tower outlasts every drawing of it. Then, underneath, in smaller letters, she listed the seven from both her lists, and beside three of them wrote the names of the drawings they would replace. The three she cut were the three she had made to impress Kurt's older brother, back when she'd wanted someone to see her working. She had liked being seen. She was less sure, now, that liking it made the drawings worth keeping, and she said so out loud, to Kinsley, who shrugged and said, "That's allowed, I think."

Her grandmother came out with sandwiches at one o'clock, surveyed the porch without comment, and moved one teacup so the wind wouldn't take a page. In her day, she said, the schools had tried to inculcate a single proper way of drawing, and she had spent forty years unlearning it; she said this the way she said everything about her past, flat and brief, while she straightened a corner that didn't need straightening. Brooklyn rolled the three rejected drawings and set them inside the door, not in the bin, not in the portfolio. She left the print book open to the wave.

Later, after the others had gone, she sat on the steps with a fresh sheet and began the tower again from memory: the water tower at dusk, seen from her grandmother's roof, a shape she had never once drawn, just to see what it would do.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll: 200 people out of a 1,000-person sample carry a margin of about plus or minus 7 points.
story:
The poll had been open in a browser tab for two days, and Kayla had spent most of those two days avoiding it. Now it was eleven at night, her deadline was in eleven hours, and the desk lamp made a small fjord of light on an otherwise dark sea of desk: a cold mug, a bag of pretzels, a printout of the school paper's style sheet. She was writing a piece for the paper's website about how voters her age were breaking, and she had found the perfect number. Among respondents aged eighteen to twenty-four, support for the transit ballot measure had dropped nine points since spring. Nine points. That was a headline. That was the whole argument, gift-wrapped.

She typed the lede twice, deleted it once, and typed it again. "Young voters are turning against the transit measure." Then she opened the poll's methodology page, mostly out of habit, the way she checked the oven was off. The full survey had talked to 1,000 people. Her slice of it, the eighteen to twenty-fours, was 200 of those. She scrolled for the margin of error and found it printed, almost bashfully, in a smaller font. The whole poll carried a margin of error of about plus or minus three points. But a subgroup inside a poll has a larger margin of error than the whole poll, and her 200 people, out of the 1,000-person sample, carried a margin of about plus or minus seven points.

She sat back. The chair made its dying-chair noise. Nine-point drop, plus or minus seven. She said the numbers out loud to the empty room, which made them sound worse, and then better, and then just strange. Somewhere between a two-point real decline and sixteen points of it, the truth lived, refusing to pick a side.

She texted Jaxen, who was awake because Jaxen was always awake. "Am I an idiot? Look at my draft." Then she called Andy, who answered on the fourth ring with the noncommittal hello of someone who did not know what time it was. She read him the headline. He said it matched his gut, actually, everyone at the skate park hated the measure. She asked how many people at the skate park. He counted, she could hear him counting. "Six," he said. "Seven if you count the guy who just nodded." She told him she had a poll of 200 and couldn't say what she wanted to say with it, and he said that was funny, and she said it was not funny, and he said no, it was kind of funny.

Her mother passed the doorway in a bathrobe and said, without stopping, "Don't stay up all night pathologizing a spreadsheet." Kayla shouted after her that it wasn't a spreadsheet, it was democracy, and got no answer but the sound of the kettle. On the screen Jaxen's reply came in, one word: "hmm."

Jaxen read the draft again at his own desk, knees against the drawer he never opened, the fan on because his window didn't. He could see exactly what Kayla had done because he would have done it too. The paragraph on young voters was the best writing in the piece, which was the problem. It was confident and musical and built on a foundation of sand, or worse, of nothing.
