He typed, "Your lede is doing math it can't afford," and then deleted it because it sounded like a fortune cookie. He typed, "Nine-point drop, seven-point margin," and left it at that. Then he added, "You could write it as the question instead of the answer." He looked at his own article from last month, the one about the cafeteria, and did not examine it too closely.

The phone buzzed against Kayla's wrist. She read Jaxen's message, then read her own lede out loud one more time, and heard it the way a stranger would hear it: certain. She opened a new document and started over. In the morning, before first period, she knocked on the door of the newsroom, where Ms. Russo was untangling a box of Ethernet cables as though it were a form of meditation. Kayla put the printed draft on the desk and pointed at the third paragraph. "I couldn't claim the drop," she said. "So I wrote that we can't tell yet, and that anyone who says they can is overselling. Two hundred of the thousand, so the margin's around seven points, plus or minus. The whole poll's is three."

Ms. Russo read the paragraph without expression, which was her version of applause. "Good. Boring, but good." She set the page down. "Boring is what honesty looks like at eleven p.m., unfortunately." Kayla said she'd found a way to keep some of the life in it, one quote from a nineteen-year-old respondent the pollster had forwarded her, and Ms. Russo said send it, and turned back to the cables.

The piece went up at lunch. Andy found her at her locker to complain that the headline was now some hedge like "Split Signals Among Young Voters," and that nobody clicked on a headline like that. "Exactly," said Kayla. "Mission accomplished." Jaxen, leaning against the doorframe, scrolled the story on his phone, past the fjord photo that served, for reasons no one could defend, as the transit measure's official promotional image. At the bottom, under her byline, the numbers sat in plain view: 200 out of 1,000, seven points either way. "You know this means the cafeteria article has a problem too," he said. Kayla closed her locker very slowly.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
Christian's grandfather had shipped the style guide in a padded envelope with a note that read, "This got me through university. Everything you need is in Chapter 15." The book was the fourteenth edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, its spine cracked, its cover the beige of old milk, and Christian had carried it to Mr. Swampy's third-period seminar because the research paper was due Friday and he had no idea how to cite anything.

The assignment had seemed simple for exactly one day. Twelve hundred words on whether his city should tear down the elevated highway that cut the east side in half, with an argument, footnotes, and a bibliography in Chicago style. Then Christian had discovered that "an argument" meant something narrower and stranger than an opinion. Mr. Swampy had circled his draft's opening sentence, "The highway is a complicated issue," and written in the margin, "Complicated is not a claim. What do you say?"

In the library during lunch, Victoria slid into the chair across from him and peered at the open manual. "What's ibid.?" she asked, tapping a page where the word appeared again and again, like a small bird hopping through the text.

"It means the same source as the one before," Christian said. "My grandfather used it for everything. It saves you writing the whole citation out twice."

"That's so efficient," Victoria said, with genuine admiration, and copied the pattern onto her own notecard about drainage systems.

Christian spent that evening footnoting happily, the rhythm of it almost soothing: full citation, then ibid., then a page number, then ibid. again. His grandfather's system felt like an inheritance, a way of writing that had carried a whole generation of Swampy-like professors through their theses. He fell asleep pleased with himself, and on Thursday morning he handed in two paragraphs early, hoping to allay his worst fear, which was that the argument itself was still a puddle of "on the one hand, on the other."

Mr. Swampy read the pages during silent work, and Christian watched his pen hover, then strike. Beside the third ibid. the pen wrote, "Where is this from?"

"Chicago," Christian said, when the seminar ended and the room had nearly emptied. He held up the beige book. "Fourteenth edition."

Mr. Swampy turned it over in his hands with something that looked like affection, then set it down. "The seventeenth edition came out in 2017," he said. "It started discouraging ibid. You repeat the author and a short title instead."

Christian stared at his footnotes, all those little birds now apparently extinct. "So my grandfather's book is wrong?"

"It's not wrong. It's old." Mr. Swampy tapped the cover once. "Fix it tonight. Paper's due at the start of class tomorrow, and I don't grade two citation systems."

At home, Christian sat between the two books, his grandfather's and the library's newer one, open to the same section, and felt the specific vertigo of discovering that a rule could change. He had assumed citation was like arithmetic, fixed forever, when it was more like language, alive and revising itself. He hunted through the seventeenth edition, found the shortened form, and began converting: Naden, Tunnels, 44. Naden, Tunnels, 51. It was more work, but he noticed something odd as he typed. Repeating the author's name made him see how much he was leaning on one source, and the imbalance of it bothered him in a way the ibids had hidden.

He called Ada, who had written her paper on urban heat islands two weeks early, because she kept a running bibliography as she read rather than at the end.

"How many sources did you use?" he asked.

"Eleven. Why?"

"I have three. One of them is from 1968." He looked at the highway department report on his screen, its optimistic prose about progress and clear sightlines. There was a tenable argument in favor of keeping the road, and a tenable argument against, and he had been hiding from choosing by stacking one historian's paragraphs on top of each other, ibid after ibid, the repetition itself a kind of camouflage.

He worked until one in the morning, found two more recent studies, and wrote a new opening sentence: "The city should replace the elevated highway with a surface boulevard, because the road's original purpose, moving freight quickly, no longer exists." He still wasn't sure about the small businesses along the route, and he said so in a paragraph near the end, plainly, without pretending the uncertainty away. That honesty felt riskier than any claim.

On Friday he submitted the paper, and the exhilaration lasted through lunch. Then Victoria found him by the lockers, holding her draft, her face drained. "Mr. Swampy marked all over mine," she said. "Every citation. He says ibid. is outdated, that the new edition doesn't want it anymore." She looked up. "Where did I even learn that?"

Christian took the notecard she was holding, the one she had copied from him, from his grandfather's book, in the library, while he had explained it so confidently. He looked at her neat handwriting, the little word doing exactly what he had told her it did, in exactly the edition he had trusted.

"I'll show you the new way," he said. "It's actually better. You just repeat the author and a short title."

Victoria frowned at her thirty ibids. "So your grandfather's book got me a B minus?"

"Technically," Christian said, "it got us both until 2017."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: The term 'unreliable narrator' was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction.
story:
Coralie got the window seat on the 7:14 bus, which mattered, because the essay was due third period and she still did not know what she thought. The prompt sat at the top of her notebook in Ms. Aquino's tidy handwriting: Who is telling you this, and why should you doubt them? Below it, three pages of her own handwriting about the novel's narrator, a charming liar named Mrs. Farraday, and every paragraph ended in a question she had crossed out.

Ishaan dropped into the seat beside her with his bag on his lap like a tray. He leaned over and read the prompt upside down, which he claimed was a skill. "Easy," he said. "Mrs. Farraday is an unreliable narrator. Done. Two thousand words."

"That's the term, but I don't know if I believe it yet." She turned back a page. "She lies about the garden. She lies about her sister. But then she tells us she lies, right at the start, so is she still unreliable, or is she playing a game with us?"

"You're overcomplicating a compliment."

A flashback arrived the way they do, without permission: Tuesday, in Ms. Aquino's room after the last bell, the smell of whiteboard marker and the radiator ticking. Anas had read his draft aloud, finished with the phrase unreliable narrator, and Ms. Aquino had looked up in that particular way she had, half pigeon, and asked, "Where does that term come from? Who coined it?" Anas had said, blankly, "English?" and she had smiled and said nothing, which was worse than a correction. Coralie had walked home turning the question over like a stone in her pocket. She had used the phrase in three essays without ever asking who had made it up, as if terms just condense out of the air, unnamed, like weather.

Back on the bus, she said, "Ms. Aquino asked Anas where the term comes from and he didn't know, and I didn't either."

Ishaan shrugged. "It's just a word. Nobody asks who coined the word bus."

"Coin," Coralie repeated, and looked out the window at the turbid brown of the creek after rain, the water moving fast under the bridge, carrying foam and twigs and something that might have been a football. "Somebody mints a word and then everyone spends it without checking whose face is on it."

Here the seat across the aisle, and the story, briefly belonged to Ishaan. He watched Coralie write the word coin in her margin and circle it, and he thought, not for the first time, that she did this thing where a small question got into her like a splinter and she would not rest until she had worked it out whole. It was exhausting and it was the reason he sat with her on the 7:14 instead of with the boys from his street, who had opinions about everything and curiosity about nothing. He also thought about the library's reference section, which stayed open until five, and about how he had a free period after lunch.

At school, before third period, they went to the library together. The critic's name was not hard to find once Coralie thought to look for books about fiction itself rather than about the novel. There it was, in a preface, plain as a bus schedule: the term unreliable narrator was coined by the critic Wayne C. Booth, in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction. 1961. She read the sentence twice, and then a third time, copying it out word for word, because after the crossing-out of Tuesday she no longer trusted her own memory to hold anything without a rope on it.

"So it's a term with a birthday," Ishaan said, reading over her shoulder. "Older than my dad's record collection."

"Someone made it up to describe something readers had probably always felt," Coralie said. "That's the part I like. Booth didn't invent liars. He invented the label for the box we put them in."

"Deposition," Anas said, arriving at the table with his own essay, still visibly bruised by Tuesday. "That's what I'm calling Mrs. Farraday's narration. Like a deposition where the witness keeps correcting herself."

"That's not what a deposition means," Ishaan said.

"It is. Sworn testimony. She swears it's true, and it isn't, which is exactly the point." Anas looked mildly triumphant, and Coralie laughed, and then, because the laugh loosened something, she opened her notebook and started the essay again from the top.

She wrote: Mrs. Farraday confesses to lying, which ought to make her honest, and instead makes her more suspect, because a liar who announces the practice is asking for a specific kind of trust, the kind you give a magician. She wrote that readers of 1961, when Booth coined the term, needed a name for this figure because fiction had begun to lean on it so heavily that ignoring it felt like a lie of the critic's own. She wanted to historicize it, to say that readers before the term must have felt the suspicion without the handle for it, the way you can carry water in cupped hands before anyone hands you a cup. She wrote all of that, and then she wrote the honest part, the part she had been circling for two days: I still do not know whether a narrator who admits to unreliability is more or less trustworthy than one who never does. Both positions had evidence. She left the question standing at the end of the page like a door she had decided not to shut.

Ms. Aquino read it that afternoon with a pen she never seemed to use. At the bottom she wrote one line: "Better question than answer. See me." Coralie read it on the bus home, in the same window seat, the creek running clearer now that the rain had stopped, and she folded the page along its crease and put it in her pocket next to the stone she was still, in some sense, carrying.

"Third period tomorrow," Ishaan said, from the seat beside her. "What are you going to tell her?"

"Tell her I don't know," Coralie said, "and mean it."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A digital elevation model is a raster layer storing the ground height of each cell, which GIS uses to predict where water will flow and collect.
story:
The map covered most of the kitchen table at Grandmother's house, though it lived inside Mya's laptop: the city rendered in pale parcels, the river a blue thread off to the east, and a wash of translucent blue-green where the floodplain was drawn. Mya had promised her geography teacher she would finish the overlay project before September, and she had promised her grandmother, more quietly, that she would figure out why the insurance letter had come. Foxglove Crescent sat nearly two kilometres from the river, uphill even, or so everyone had always said, and yet the city's map insisted it lay inside the risk zone.

"Look at this," she said, turning the laptop so her grandmother could see from the stove. "Your street's darker than the ones by the bridge."

Her grandmother came over, wiping her hands, and stood in that particular way she had, weight on one hip, reading the screen as if it were a letter she'd already guessed the contents of. "We've never had water. Forty years, not a drop in the basement." She tapped the counter above the keyboard, once. "Except the spring the schoolyard went under, but that's not the river, that's just the ground being stupid."

Mya wrote that down. The ground being stupid. It was the kind of phrase her teacher would have circled and called folk knowledge, but Mya had learned that her grandmother's phrases usually pointed at something real, the way a dog points at a bird before you see it yourself.

She layered the housing data next, each parcel tinted by age and value, and the pattern made her stomach tighten: the darker the flood risk, the cheaper and older the housing, street after street, until the map looked like a bruise spreading through the east side. She took a screenshot for Xander, who was doing the same project across town, and he called within minutes.

"It's doing that on mine too," he said. "Streets nowhere near the water, flagged anyway. I asked Dale and he said his cousin's place is like that, and his cousin's furious about it." There was a pause, the sound of him eating something. "You know what it is, though? Check the digital elevation model. It's a raster layer, every cell stores the ground height. That's what the flood tool uses, to predict where water will flow and collect." He said it fast, the way he repeated things he'd just read, and she could hear the smugness arriving before he'd finished the sentence.

She found the layer and turned it on, and the city changed character entirely. The river almost vanished into irrelevance. What mattered instead was a long, shallow depression she'd never noticed in twelve years of riding her bike across it, a shallow bowl that ran from the north edge of town straight through the schoolyard, through the ball diamonds, through Foxglove Crescent, and out the other side. The ground wasn't stupid. The ground was honest, and it had been telling everyone the truth in a language nobody had bothered to translate. Water did not care about distance from the river; it cared about downhill, and downhill, on this map, ran right beneath her grandmother's kitchen.

It had taken her most of the summer, glacial progress some weeks, an hour here while her grandmother napped, an hour there after dinner, and now everything she'd built was suddenly legible at once. She thought of her parents two years ago, choosing this neighbourhood over the new development by the highway because it was "established," "on higher ground." She thought of the synchronicity of it, that she'd been assigned this project at all, that the insurance letter had come the same month, as if the universe had decided the Delgados needed the lesson twice. Then she thought, more slowly, that it probably wasn't the universe, only the city updating its models, and that the coincidence was the boring kind. She preferred the boring kind. The boring kind you could argue with.

Mr. Rossi, next door, was out trimming his hedge in the evening heat, and she carried the laptop over to show him, because he'd sat on the city's drainage committee once and she wanted to see his face when he looked at the elevation layer. He set down the shears. He leaned in. He was quiet for longer than she expected.

"Your grandmother's lot is the lowest on this street," he said finally. "Two feet lower than mine, maybe three." He straightened up and looked at his own house, then at hers, as if measuring the distance between them for the first time. "Funny thing is, when we all bought here, the salesman told us the new development by the highway was the flood risk. Flat as a table out there, he said. No drainage at all." He picked the shears back up. "Course, that was before anybody put it on a map."

That night Mya added the new development to her overlay, her parents' almost-house, the one they'd turned down. She sat very still while the layers drew themselves. Then her grandmother called from the kitchen, asking whether she wanted tea, and Mya closed the laptop halfway, screen still glowing, and said, "Grandma, do you remember the name of that development by the highway?"

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Simon Schama's Citizens, published in 1989 for the Revolution's bicentenary, argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward.
story:
The carriage house behind the Whitcomb Museum had been converted into a reading room, and it was there, under a ceiling of old hand-hewn beams, that Madison unrolled her notes on the French Revolution and discovered she had arranged them wrong. She had sorted the historians by date, which felt scholarly and orderly, but the dates told her nothing about why anyone had thought what they thought. Tristan was already at the long table with his laptop open, and Allyson arrived late, shaking rain off her jacket and apologizing to the room in general, though the room held only the three of them, a docent at the far desk, and Ms. Johansson, who had driven them here and was now deep in conversation with the docent about the provenance of a clock.

They had come to see the traveling exhibition on revolutionary France, eight cases of prints, pamphlets and a single lock of hair labeled as belonging to someone who had guarded the Tuileries. Ms. Johansson had assigned the historiographical essay before the trip: how views of the Revolution had changed since 1800, and each of them had to hold a position by Friday. Madison's draft argued that the Terror of 1793 was a detour, a wrong turn taken under wartime panic, and that the Revolution's early promise had been genuine. Tristan, naturally, argued the opposite. He was applying to study immunology in the fall and liked systems more than stories; he kept saying the violence was not an infection that struck a healthy body but something the body had carried from the beginning.

"You're both being obdurate," Allyson said, dropping into the chair between them. "That's my thesis, actually. Historiography is two people refusing to budge and calling it scholarship."

"Mine has sources," Tristan said.

At the exhibition they moved from case to case, and it was in front of the print of the storming of the Bastille that Tristan stopped and tapped the glass, though a small placard asked him not to. "Look at the date. 1789. Everyone treats this like the pure part, the good Revolution before it all went wrong. I think that's a story people needed afterward."

Madison remembered, then, her father at the kitchen table last spring, reading a review in the paper and pushing it across to her. She had been fifteen and mostly annoyed, but she had read it, because it was about a book that had come out for the Revolution's bicentenary in 1989. She hadn't retained the argument, only the cover: a red banner, the word Citizens in white. She had assumed, at fifteen, that any book about a bicentenary would be celebratory. It had not occurred to her that a birthday book might argue something darker.

Back at the table she scrolled the museum's catalog on her laptop, and there it was. Simon Schama, Citizens, 1989. She read the summary twice, then a third time, her finger moving along the screen as though the words might rearrange themselves.

"Listen," she said. "Simon Schama's Citizens, published in 1989 for the bicentenary, argued that violence was an essential part of the Revolution from 1789 onward." She said it slowly, the way she repeated lines she wanted to keep. "From the start. Not 1793. 1789."

"So I was right," Tristan said, but he said it without his usual relish, watching her face instead of savoring the win.

"That's not what it means." Madison pulled her draft toward her and looked at the paragraph where she had called the Terror a detour, a betrayal of 1789's innocence. The sentence sat there looking thinner than it had at two in the morning in her bedroom. "It means the detour theory has a rival, and the rival has a serious book behind it, and my essay can't just wave it away."

Allyson leaned over. "Then don't pick. That's the whole point of the assignment, isn't it? It's not asking what the Revolution was. It's asking what people thought it was."

"It's asking what I think," Madison said. But saying it aloud made it smaller and more possible. She had been treating the essay like a verdict, one she had to deliver without doubt, and doubt had felt like failure. Ms. Johansson had said something like that in class in September, on the day Madison had asked whether an essay could be wrong. "A considered position can hold uncertainty," Ms. Johansson had said, "as long as it's honest about where the uncertainty sits." Madison had written it in the margin of her notebook and then never looked at it again.

She turned to a fresh page. At the top she wrote the question she actually had: why had Schama, writing at the bicentenary, when everyone else was marking two hundred years with fireworks and conferences, chosen to argue that the violence was there from the beginning? She wrote a line about her father and the review, then crossed it out as too personal, then wrote it again smaller. She would set the two views side by side, the older one that mourned a betrayed beginning and Schama's that denied the beginning had ever been innocent, and she would say which she found more persuasive and where she still couldn't tell.

"Can I see?" Tristan asked. She slid the notebook across. He read it, frowning, and she braced herself.

"You're going to say the detour thing is dead," she said.

"No. I'm going to say you stole my thesis and made it better." He handed it back. "Mine's just an argument. Yours is an argument about arguments."

Allyson had wandered to the window, where the rain had stopped and the wet gravel of the courtyard was going bright at the edges. "The docent says they're lighting the carriage lamps at five," she said. "Like it would have been. Come look."

Madison closed the notebook, and the three of them stood at the glass while the lamps came on one by one along the drive, each flame small and steady in its black iron cage.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: The genetic code is read in codons of three bases; there are 64 possible codons but only 20 standard amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon.
story:
Mr. Janssen had said the quiz would take twenty minutes, and I finished in ten, which proved I knew the material. The quiz covered transcription and translation, the whole path from DNA to protein, and I had written it out cleanly: the DNA strand opens, RNA polymerase builds a messenger RNA copy, the messenger travels to the ribosome, and the ribosome reads it in groups of three bases and matches each group to an amino acid. I had not copied any of it from Nadia's worksheet, no matter what she would later claim. Her worksheet was upside down from where I sat and unreadable besides.

After the quizzes went in, Mr. Janssen set out the codon charts, one laminated square per table, and told us to translate a sequence he wrote on the board, base by base, into its amino acids. This was the part I actually liked. The chart was printed like a grid, bases down the side and across the top, and you traced your fingers along the rows until they met in a little box with an abbreviation in it. Leu. Val. Ser. It felt less like biology than like using a map, or like those puzzle books my grandmother kept by her chair.

Nadia sat across from me tracing the same sequence, and Marguerite sat beside her, chewing her pen. Marguerite was only in the class because her mother wanted her to study physiology someday, which Marguerite described as "cutting people open for money," and she had recently tried to monetize her lab notes by selling photocopies to students in the other section. Mr. Janssen had found out. He had not been florid about it, which was somehow worse; he had just said, "Marguerite, see me after class," and she had gone pale and stayed pale.

The sequence on the board broke into groups of three, and I worked down the line. ATA. GGG. TTT. My fingers moved across the grid and stopped. I checked the row again. Then I checked the row above it.

"Nadia," I said. "What did you get for the second one? The GGG."

"Proline," she said. "Wait. No. I got proline for the fourth one too, and the fourth one is CCG. That can't be right. GGG and CCG aren't the same."

I traced both. GGG gave proline. CCG also gave proline. I slid the chart over to her so we could be wrong together, which is what working in a lab is, mostly.

"They're the same," Nadia said. "Two different codons, same amino acid." She counted the boxes along one row of the chart, her pen tip ticking against the lamination. "There are sixty-four of these. Sixty-four possible codons."

"Sixty-four and only twenty amino acids on the whole chart," Marguerite said, leaning over. She had not been participating until the chart stopped behaving, and now she was interested, pen abandoned. "So most of these amino acids have more than one codon. That's why we kept landing in the same box."

I said I had known that already, and at the time I believed it. I had certainly seen the chart before, in the textbook, in the chapter I had read twice, and it was possible I had noticed the repetitions and filed them somewhere. But the truth, which I admitted to no one at that table, was that I had expected the code to be tidy. One codon, one amino acid, a clean key. The redundancy felt like an insult to the system, and also like the system knowing something I didn't, and I did not enjoy the second feeling.

Mr. Janssen came by our table and looked at our papers. Nadia showed him the two codons, GGG and CCG, and said, "Both of these code for proline. Is the chart broken?" He said the chart was fine, picked up a stool, sat down, and asked us what we thought that meant for a mutation. That was all he said, and then he waited, which was his way of making you do the work.

Marguerite got there first. "If a base changes and the new codon still means the same amino acid," she said slowly, "the protein doesn't change. The mutation doesn't do anything."

"So it's not broken," I said. "It's protected." I heard myself say it and recognized, with some irritation, that it was a real thought, arrived at in the last four minutes, in the middle of a class I had claimed to have mastered an hour ago. Nadia was already copying the next sequence from the board, and Marguerite had taken her pen back out of her mouth and was drawing a line through every duplicated amino acid on the chart, one at a time, like she was crossing off a list of debts.

"One to eleven," she said, counting the codons for leucine. "One amino acid, eleven codons. Somebody should be paying me for this."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
The rain had been falling since four, and Tristan told himself it was good conditions, really, the kind of conditions that made a first lesson worth something. His mother slid into the passenger seat with the keys and said nothing about the weather, which he took as agreement. The car was her old one, a spartan hatchback with a cracked dashboard and no screen of any kind, and she had made him check the mirrors twice before letting him turn the ignition.

"Country road," she said. "Less to hit." She said it lightly, but her hand found the door handle and stayed there, and Tristan noticed and pretended not to.

He pulled out of the driveway too fast, corrected, and told himself it had been a smooth exit. The wipers thumped at their slowest setting because he couldn't find the second notch, and for a while he didn't ask. The road ran out past the grain elevator and narrowed to two wet lanes with gravel shoulders, ditches brimming brown on both sides. Rain silvered the asphalt in the headlights. He was doing fifty and holding the wheel the way Ms. Siddiqui had told him to hold his pen in the exam, loose at nine and three, when he remembered it, and loosened his grip.

Two nights before, Kane had gesticulated wildly across a cafeteria tray, re-enacting his cousin's crash on Route 9. "Hit standing water, and the whole car just floats," Kane had said, arms wide, a small aircraft taking off above the milk cartons. "Like you're driving on air. Nothing you do matters." Tristan had laughed at the performance. He thought about it now, briefly, and decided Kane exaggerated everything, always had, and that the road ahead was merely wet, not dangerous. He kept his foot steady.

Where the road dipped under the rail line, a shallow sheet of water lay black across both lanes, longer than it looked. He saw it late. His mother said, "Careful," and he steered a little, which was a mistake, and then the steering went weightless in his hands. The wheel turned as if it were no longer connected to anything. The car drifted left, toward the center line, gently, the way a canoe drifts when nobody is paddling.

"Tristan." His mother's voice was flat and quick.

He gripped harder and turned the wheel more. Nothing happened. The car kept drifting. There was a moment, half a second, when he understood that nothing he did with the steering was reaching the road, and in that half second he heard Kane again, arms out, saying it floats, and for once Kane was not exaggerating. He also heard his own voice in his head saying I had it under control, which he knew, even then, was the first lie of the evening.

He took his foot off the accelerator. Not a decision exactly; his leg did it, the way a hand pulls back from a stove. The engine noise dropped, the car slowed on its own, and then the wheel came back to him. He felt it return, a weight re-entering the tires, and the car tracked straight again through the last of the water and up the far side of the dip. His hands were shaking. He did not mention the hands.

"What was that?" his mother asked.

"Hydroplaning," he said. "The water builds up between the tires and the road. You lose traction." He had not known the word two minutes ago; now he was handing it to her like it was his. "Kane told me his cousin did it. He said you can't steer. He was right about that part."

"So what fixed it?"

"Easing off the gas. The tires get their grip back." He said it plainly, without dressing it up, because she would have heard the dressing. He slowed the car to forty and turned the wipers up two notches, finding the switch on the second try, and the windshield cleared as if the whole evening were being wiped too.

They drove on. At the next crossroads a porch light burned at Ms. Siddiqui's place, and her dog came to the fence and paced them along the wire, and Tristan signaled and turned left, properly, early, because he wanted one thing in the evening to be unambiguous. He was quiet for most of the road home, and the truth assembled itself slowly, the way the rain assembled in the ditches. His mother would report to his father that he had handled it, and that version was partly true; he had lifted his foot at the right instant, and the tires had found the road again. But he had also gone into standing water at fifty with the wipers barely working, and if his leg had not moved on its own he did not know what his mind would have chosen, because in the moment his mind had been holding the wheel and shouting at it. Both of those were true at once. He could not make them into one clean story, and he was tired of the version Kane would hear at school tomorrow, so he decided not to supply it.

Back in the driveway, engine off, rain ticking on the roof, his mother said, "Same time Thursday?" She was already unbuckling.

"In the rain again?"

"Forecast looks better," she said. "But we'll go through that dip either way. You should do it until it's boring."

He watched her cross the lawn to the porch, her keys in her fist, and sat a moment longer with his hands still at nine and three. "Until it's boring," he repeated to the empty car, and turned the wipers off.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
Robert found the envelope on Monday, propped against the printer in the student newspaper office like a piece of sedimentary rock deposited there by some slow, indifferent force. It was from Halvorsen Chevrolet, which had bought the back page of the Westbrook High Ledger for longer than anyone currently on staff had been alive. The letter said, in two sentences, that the dealership would not be renewing its advertising, and that it wished the paper well. It did not mention the editorial from three weeks ago, the one about the school board handing the drivers' education contract to a company that happened to be owned by Halvorsen's brother-in-law.

"They can't just do that," Brianne said, reading the letter upside down across the desk. The office smelled of toner and the cold pizza Ricardo kept in the mini fridge with the broken door.

"They can do whatever they want," Ricardo said. "It's their money." He said it lightly, the way he said most things, but he was the business manager, and he had already done the arithmetic in his head. Robert could tell because Ricardo's pencil was moving before anyone had asked him anything.

Mr. Whitehead came in during fifth period with his coffee and his habit of standing by the window as though supervising the parking lot. He read the letter, put it down, and said only, "Well. You wanted to run a newspaper." Then he assigned Robert a feature for the next issue, which was Mr. Whitehead's way of not discussing something.

That night Robert called his grandfather, who watched television news with the devotion other men reserved for golf. Robert had gone to him originally to ask about advertising, since his grandfather had owned a hardware store for forty years and had opinions about every business in the county. But the conversation drifted, as it did, backward.

"You know it wasn't always like this," his grandfather said. "There was a thing called the fairness doctrine. Nineteen forty-nine. Broadcasters had to air contrasting views on controversial public issues. The FCC abolished it in eighty-seven." He said it the way he recited the price of a hammer in 1974, a fact that had settled into him permanently.

"On TV," Robert said. "Not newspapers."

"On TV," his grandfather agreed. "But you take my meaning." Robert was not entirely sure he did, though he liked the sound of the old rule, the idea of a referee standing somewhere offscreen. He looked it up later anyway, half expecting his grandfather to have invented it, and found the dates intact: introduced 1949, abolished 1987, and between those years a stretch of time when the airwaves had been obliged to hold two ideas at once. His grandfather had not invented it. This was itself a little unsettling.

The next afternoon the office was warm and the window was open, letting in the smell of cut grass from the practice field. Brianne had drafted a story about the lost ad, and it read like a battle report. "They're punishing us," she insisted, tapping the page. "Everyone will know it. That's the point of running it."

"That's the point for you," Ricardo said. He had the budget spreadsheet open, and its numbers had a bluntness no editorial could match. The Ledger needed four hundred dollars a month it did not currently have. "Print the story and we lose the pharmacy too, probably. My uncle says businesses talk."

Robert sat between them, literally, because the third chair was between theirs, and tried to hold both positions the way the fairness doctrine apparently used to make broadcasters do. Brianne's side was clean and true: a paper that softened itself for advertisers wasn't a paper. Ricardo's side was also true, and it was true in a way that could not be extenuated by any amount of principle, because principle did not buy newsprint. He said as much, badly, out loud, and both of them looked at him with the particular patience people reserve for someone trying to be fair.

"Being fair isn't a story," Brianne said.

"Maybe it's a policy," Robert said. He pulled the draft toward himself and began cutting. The new version kept the facts, the letter, the dates, the brother-in-law, but it lost the word "punishment" and gained a paragraph quoting the dealership's manager, who had not returned any calls yet but who might. "We print what happened. We don't print what we think it means."

"That's cowardice wearing a tie," Brianne said, but she was rereading it, and she did not cross anything out.

Mr. Whitehead read the revised story on Thursday, standing by the window with his coffee going cold. He was quiet long enough that Robert began composing a defense in his head. Whether the fairness doctrine would have applied to them, Robert still didn't know; it had been about broadcasters, about the public air, and a school paper paid for by a Chevrolet dealership sat somewhere outside its borders. He suspected, though he had not decided, that the old rule had been a guardrail for a road they weren't on, and that they were on a worse road, one where the referees were sponsors. He kept that to himself.

Mr. Whitehead set the page down. "Run it," he said. "And Ricardo, ask the pharmacy if they want the back page." Then he went to the window again, and outside, someone had painted the end zone stripes crooked, and three players stood looking at them, none of them moving to fix it.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
story:
Blake spread the postcard reproduction of Frida Kahlo's "The Two Fridas" on the picnic table and weighted its corners with stones, because the August wind kept lifting it like something trying to escape. He had a notebook, a pencil, and one evening before the assignment was due: a formal analysis of colour, composition, symbolism, three pages, no biographical padding. Ms. Bondarenko had written "describe what you see, then argue what it means" on the board, and Blake had copied it down as though it were a spell whose powers he did not yet trust.

Matthew dropped onto the bench across from him with a can of soda and pulled the postcard closer without asking. "This is the one with the two versions of herself, right? Exposed hearts, one in white, one in blue. That's pretty Surrealist, if you ask me."

"I didn't ask you," Blake said, but without heat, because he had written the same word in his margin an hour ago and then crossed it out, and the crossing out bothered him more than the writing had.

Fanny arrived with her own copy of the painting, a library book open to a full plate, and set it beside his postcard so they could compare the scale of things. "My critique called her a Surrealist too," she said. "I got it back with a note. Breton described Kahlo's art as 'a ribbon around a bomb.'" She said it flatly, reading from her returned page. "But Kahlo herself rejected the Surrealist label. She said she didn't paint dreams."

Matthew leaned back. "Then Breton got her wrong?"

"Or he got her wrong in a useful way," Blake said slowly. He was looking at the ribbon, the actual ribbon, the artery that the Frida in white holds with her own fingers, looping between the two hearts. A decorative thing, delicate, doing the work of connection. He thought about how a man looking at a woman's paintings had reached for an ornament wrapped around violence, and how the woman had looked at her own paintings and reached for a different word entirely. Both descriptions circled the same canvases. Only one of them had to live inside the body in the painting.

"Say that again," Fanny said, "but like a sentence you'd actually hand in."

He tried. The colours first, because that was the discipline of it: the storm grey of the sky, the cold white dress, the warmer teal of the traditional dress, the red of the two hearts and the thin line of blood dropping toward the hem, the tiny portrait held in one hand. The composition held the two figures joined at the arm, nearly symmetrical, nearly centred, so that nothing in the arrangement felt accidental even when it felt impossible. The symbolism was where the arguing started. "The exposed heart isn't fantasy," Blake said, testing it aloud. "It's anatomy used as an argument. She painted her insides as facts."

"So where does that leave the bomb line?" Matthew asked, spinning the soda can in a slow circle.

Blake wrote two columns in his notebook and put Breton's phrase at the top of one and Kahlo's rejection at the top of the other, and found he could not fill either column cleanly, because each kept leaking into the other. The Surrealist framing made the painting sound like an enigma to be decoded, and Blake did not want to decode it; he wanted to say what the grey sky did to the red, how the symmetry gave the double self a kind of gravitas that a single figure would not have carried, how the little portrait was the only object in the picture that was not also flesh. He also suspected, in a way he could not yet support, that calling her a Surrealist made her easier to sell, easier to commodify, a curiosity rather than a painter in control of every decision on the canvas. But that was a suspicion, not a finding, and Ms. Bondarenko would see the difference.

"It's germane to the analysis," Fanny said, tapping the book. "The dispute, I mean. You can put both positions in the paper and still take one."

"I know it's germane," Blake said. "That's the problem. I can take hers because she painted it, or his because it's beautiful, and I can't tell if the beautiful one is also the true one." He looked at the postcard, where the wind had shifted one stone and the corner fluttered, lifting the white dress a fraction of an inch off the table. He reached out and pressed it flat with his palm, and left his hand there while the sky behind the two Fridas went on being grey.

Matthew drained his soda and stood. "So write it from her side and admit what you can't settle. That's allowed, right?"

Fanny pulled the library book back and began copying the citation into her phone. Blake turned to a fresh page and wrote, at the top, "The Two Fridas: colour, composition, and a dispute about a name." Under it, after a moment, he wrote, "a ribbon around a bomb," and then, beneath that, in smaller letters, "but she rejected the label," and he underlined nothing, letting the two lines sit there side by side.

story:
The argument started over a lab bench that smelled of vinegar and something the period before them had spilled and never wiped up. Mahdi had his phone out, holding it toward Hunter like evidence at a trial. "Twelve kids," he said. "Twelve kids got the shot, and then twelve kids got diagnosed. That's the whole study. My cousin sent it to me."

Hunter took the phone, though he already knew he would hate whatever was on it. He was the one who had gotten the class into this. Two days ago, in a moment he had regretted almost immediately, he had told Ms. Mansour that his little brother's appointment for the MMR booster had been moved because their mother kept circling the same articles online, growing more certain with each one. Ms. Mansour had not lectured him. She had only said, "Bring it to class if you want. Sometimes a claim is easier to look at with other people around." Now here they were, Wednesday, fourth period, a debate nobody had agreed to have, and Hunter had walked in with a folder of printouts because he wanted, more than he could calmly admit, to have something his mother couldn't scroll past.

"Twelve," Mahdi repeated, tapping the screen. "That's a pattern, bro."

"It's a small one," Hunter said. He heard how that sounded, like a retreat, and Mahdi heard it too, because he leaned back on his stool with the satisfaction of someone who has already won.

Yacine, who sat near the window and usually spent labs half-listening, turned around in his chair. "Wait," he said. "Hold on. Twelve? My mom's a nurse. She says the one everyone talks about is huge. Like a whole country huge." He frowned at the ceiling, trying to pull the number out of it. "Denmark, I think. She brought it up at dinner because my aunt was being difficult about my little cousins."

Hunter set Mahdi's phone down on the bench, screen still glowing, and opened his folder. He had printed pages the night before in the school library, dog-earing corners, reading the same paragraphs twice because he did not trust himself to get the numbers right. "Danish study," he said. "Published in 2019. They followed more than 650,000 children." He let that sit for a second, because the size of it deserved a second. "No link between the MMR vaccine and autism. Not even among kids who already had autistic siblings."

"Six hundred fifty thousand," Yacine said slowly, as if tasting it. "And twelve." He looked at Mahdi, not unkindly. "My mom would say that's not even the same sport."

Mahdi crossed his arms, and for a moment he looked ready to become bellicose about it, chin out, voice climbing. "So a big study beats a small one automatically? That's just, like, popularity."

"No," Hunter said, and he surprised himself with how quickly the word came. "It's not about size being popular. It's about what happens after." He pulled out another page, the one he had read three times on the bus. "One study isn't the end of anything. Other people check it. They try the same question different ways. If it keeps coming out the same, over and over, that's when people start agreeing. It's not one guy with a result. It's a lot of people failing to break it." He turned the page toward Mahdi. "That part's called replication. It's in here somewhere."

Ms. Mansour, who had been ostensibly writing something at her desk across the room, drifted over with the fake casualness of a teacher who had been listening the whole time. She did not explain anything. She only picked up Mahdi's phone, glanced at it, set it back down, and said, "You two could design a controlled experiment for the unit project. Figure out what would convince you." Then she moved on to unstack beakers, leaving them with it.

Mahdi was quiet for most of the rest of the period. Hunter watched him copy the name of the Danish study into his notebook, slowly, checking the spelling twice, and Hunter understood that his mother would not be convinced by a folder of printouts, not this week, maybe not this year. He was honest with himself about that. But he also understood that Mahdi writing it down was its own kind of thing, small and real, and that a person could believe a number and still take years to act on it. At the bell, Yacine clapped Mahdi on the shoulder and said, "Tell your cousin dinner's on me if she can find a bigger study." Mahdi almost smiled. He zipped the phone into his bag, then, at the door, he paused. "Hey, Hunter," he said. "That number. Six fifty thousand. Say it again."
